before_object.statement: Use the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and SI conventions of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], fix $K>0$, $\omega:=cK$, $k:=Ke_3$ (so $|k|=\omega/c$), and let $E_0>0$ carry the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$. For each amplitude choice below put $b:=k\times e/\omega$, so that the amplitude equations of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold and the corresponding fields are smooth source-free vacuum Maxwell solutions on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. (i) [Linear] $e:=E_0e_1$, $b=(E_0/c)e_2$: here $a=E_0e_1$, $d=0$, the trace is the segment $[-E_0,E_0]e_1=\{s e_1:-E_0\le s\le E_0\}$ traversed twice per period, the polarisation is linear and $H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle=0$; $E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$, $B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$, and $|B|=|E|/c$. actual_supplier.title: Polarization of a transverse plane wave: linear, circular and elliptical traces, and handedness
actual_supplier.statement: Let $(E,B)$ be a plane-wave pair of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] with wavevector $k\ne0$, angular frequency $\omega>0$ and complex amplitudes $e,b$, and suppose the amplitude conditions of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold, so that $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$. If the pair is nonzero, they also imply $|k|=\omega/c$; the zero pair is permitted for every $k\ne0$, $\omega>0$, both on and off this dispersion relation. This item is a classification definition for that class of transverse plane waves; it adds no field-theoretic content. Write $e=a+id$ with the real vectors $a=\operatorname{Re}e$, $d=\operatorname{Im}e$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), so that $k\cdot a=k\cdot d=0$; let $\hat k=k/|k|$, and use $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $\times$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Then: (a) [Trace] At fixed $x$ the electric vector is $E(x,t)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$, and the curve $\gamma(\theta):=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ lies in the transverse plane $k^\perp=\{v: k\cdot v=0\}$. It is the image of the unit circle under the linear map $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$, it is closed with phase-parameter period $2\pi$, while $t\mapsto E(x,t)$ has time period $T=2\pi/\omega$, and $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$. It is called the **polarisation trace** at $x$; the classification below is independent of $x$. (b) [Classification] (i) **Linear polarisation**: $\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$; when $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the trace is a nontrivial segment in that span traversed twice per period; when $a=d=0$, the trace is the single point $\{0\}$ and the fields are the zero wave. (ii) **Circular polarisation**: $|a|=|d|>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$; the trace is the circle of radius $|a|$ in $k^\perp$, and $|E(x,t)|=|a|$ for all $(x,t)$. (iii) **Elliptical (nondegenerate, noncircular) polarisation**: $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$ and not (ii); the trace is a nondegenerate ellipse centred at $0$ with the origin in its interior. If $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the parametrisation is along principal axes and the semiaxes have lengths $|a|$ and $|d|$; the general principal-axis computation is not asserted by this item. (c) [Handedness] For $a,d\in k^\perp$ the cross product $a\times d$ is parallel to $\hat k$, so the **helicity sign** $H:=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle\in\mathbb R$ vanishes exactly in the linear case (i) and is nonzero otherwise ([[def-real-order]] for its sign). This library calls the polarisation **right-handed** when $H<0$ and **left-handed** when $H>0$. Geometrically, $H<0$ means the electric vector at fixed $x$ rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing the incoming wave (looking along $-\hat k$), and $H>0$ means counterclockwise. Here the screen orientation is fixed by any positive orthonormal triad $(u,v,\hat k)$, with $u$ to the right and $v$ up for this observer; equivalently $\langle E\times\partial_tE,\hat k\rangle=\omega H$. This fixes the sign convention of the cited treatment (there: $E_0=\alpha-i\beta$, right-handed iff $\beta=\hat k\times\alpha$, which under $a=\alpha$, $d=-\beta$ is $H=-|a|^2<0$ in the circular case). The names 'right' and 'left' handedness are conventional and both conventions occur in the literature, so later statements in this library use only the sign of $H$. (d) [Status] This is a classification definition: it introduces the trace, the three cases and the sign $H$, and asserts no field equation, no propagation, energy or empirical content. The magnetic amplitude enters only through the transverse relations recalled above.
actual_supplier.strategy: An explicit classification definition. The transverse conditions $k\cdot a=k\cdot d=0$ are the real and imaginary parts of $k\cdot e=0$ from [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]. The trace formula is the elementary rewriting $\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+id)e^{i\theta}\bigr)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]); closedness and the reflection symmetry are immediate from the circular functions of the encoding definition. In (b)(iii), independence of $a,d$ makes $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ injective, so the trace is a linearly embedded circle (an ellipse) around the origin: the origin lies inside because the image of the compact unit circle is a curve encircling $0$ under an injective linear map. In (c), $a\times d$ is orthogonal to $a$ and $d$ and hence parallel to $k$ ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), so $H=0$ exactly when $a\times d=0$, i.e. in the linear case; the rotation identity follows by differentiating $E=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\partial_t\theta=-\omega$, giving $E\times\partial_tE=\omega a\times d$. For example, $\hat k=e_3$ and $e=e_1-ie_2$ give $E(0,t)=\cos(\omega t)e_1-\sin(\omega t)e_2$, clockwise in the specified screen orientation. The naming convention is fixed as stated and matches the cited treatment under the dictionary $a=\alpha$, $d=-\beta$. The principal-axis caveat is recorded because the general diagonalisation is not part of this item's strategy. No field equation or physical claim is introduced.

## Definition

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

## Remarks

- **Scope: the concrete form only.** What is defined above is the Euclidean inner
  product on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and nothing more. The general theory of inner
  product spaces — abstract inner products, orthonormal bases, Gram-Schmidt,
  orthogonal projection and orthogonal complements of arbitrary subspaces — is
  planned for a page of this library that comes **earlier in the plan order** and
  is not yet built. No item on this page claims anything about abstract inner
  product spaces, and no item on this page introduces the general notion.

  $e_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ has $e_i(i) = 1$ and $e_i(j) = 0$ for $j \ne i$

  coordinates of $x$ are recovered by testing against the standard basis, which

  [[thm-of-square-roots]] and [[lem-power-laws]].

actual_supplier.title: Laboratory geometry: a restricted inertial chart, its spatial slices and fixed-time fields
actual_supplier.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then: (a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and $c>0$; its components are the laboratory time coordinate $t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the laboratory position $r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. (b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice $U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the coordinates of $r$ are expressed. (c) [Laboratory fields] A laboratory field of rank $m$ is a map $F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$, $p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class $C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed $t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is asserted beyond the class stated for it. (d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer field is defined here.
actual_supplier.strategy: A construction definition with elementary verifications. The inertial chart $x$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] is a bijection, so its restriction to the set of events whose chart coordinates lie in $cI\times\Omega$ has image $cI\times\Omega$; composing with the bijection $cI\times\Omega\to I\times\Omega$, $(ct,y)\mapsto(t,y)$ (bijective because $c>0$) gives the bijection $\Phi$. Each slice $U_t$ is $\Phi^{-1}(\{t\}\times\Omega)$, on which $r$ restricts to a bijection onto $\Omega$. The claims about $n$, $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, $\delta$ and the orientation are exactly the content of [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]; the $C^k$ notion is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] and the two kinds of partial derivative are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] applied to the product coordinates. Clause (d) records conventions only: the frame dependence of $r,\delta$ and slices is stated rather than hidden, and no Galilean or observer-congruence claim is made. Nothing here uses a theorem of the framework, and the laboratory region may be a proper subset of $A$; no global chart of $A$ other than the given inertial chart is asserted.
